about.bio: AI infrastructure engineer. I build the systems underneath LLMs — retrieval pipelines, agent loops, and the Go services that keep them fast under load. Most of my work is the unglamorous half of AI: making retrieval return the right chunk, making generation reproducible, and making the whole thing survive production traffic at 3am. Currently going deeper on the inference serving layer — batching, routing, and GPU utilization.

projects.title: repi
projects.blurb: local-first log RCA · hybrid RAG · state-machine agent
projects.details: An autonomous log investigation engine that runs entirely on your own machine. It ingests distributed service logs, clusters them by signature, retrieves evidence with hybrid vector + BM25 search, and reasons through root cause in a state-machine-supervised investigation loop — no logs, no embeddings, nothing leaves the box.
projects.architecture: A background worker tails configured log directories with offset tracking, so ingestion is continuous and resumable. Logs flow through parsing, signature clustering, embedding, and upsert into Postgres — vectors into a pgvector HNSW index, text into a ParadeDB BM25 full-text index. Queries run both retrievers and fuse their rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, with query expansion for recall; results surface as timeline and cluster views. The investigation runs as an explicit state machine (resolving → sweeping → gathering ⇄ reflecting → compiling), where each gathering pass reads evidence, forms a hypothesis, and probes further — the reason-act loop is the worker step, the state machine is the supervisor that owns budgets, confidence floors, clarification pauses, and resume. A separate LLM compilation step then synthesizes the finding. Every investigation is stored with a step-by-step audit trail, and logs are partitioned into projects so services and environments stay isolated. The whole thing ships as multi-arch Docker images alongside Postgres and Redis.
design_decisions: A hand-rolled state machine over adopting LangGraph — the explicit phase graph captures roughly 80% of the structural benefit at a fraction of the migration cost, and keeps the project free of framework coupling. Around 1,400 lines of battle-tested edge cases (graduated exits, reflection gating, confidence floors, observation compaction, tool dedup) would have needed reimplementation against a custom tool protocol and adapter layer.

The state machine supervises rather than replaces the reason-act loop — root-cause analysis cannot gather all evidence up front, because the next query depends on what the last observation revealed. Gathering and reflecting form a cycle, not a pipeline, so the agent keeps choosing where to look while the supervisor owns termination.

Local-first and self-hosted with zero external dependencies — production logs are the single most sensitive text a company owns. An incident tool that ships them to a vendor's API is one nobody in a regulated org is allowed to install.

Postgres as the single store for both retrievers — pgvector for similarity, ParadeDB for BM25, one database, one transaction boundary. Logs and their embeddings can never drift apart, and there's no second system to operate.

Hybrid retrieval fused with RRF instead of vector-only — logs are dense with exact tokens (error codes, request IDs, hostnames) that embeddings blur into neighbours. RRF fuses on rank, so it needs no score normalization between two retrievers whose scores share no scale.

Progressive time-window expansion (10 → 60 → 360 → 1440 minutes) instead of one fixed window — an investigation usually starts with no known time bound. Widening in steps finds local causes fast and only pays for the wide search when the narrow one comes up empty.
A provider abstraction over OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Gemini and Ollama — no single vendor is load-bearing, and the Ollama path is what makes the local-first claim actually true end to end.
Signature clustering before embedding — the unit of meaning in logs is the template, not the line.
tradeoffs: Single-machine ceiling in exchange for operational simplicity — it runs on one box with Postgres and Redis, which caps throughput but means the install is a docker compose up rather than a platform team.

A separate LLM compilation step over answering straight out of the loop — one more call and a bit more latency, but evidence gathering and synthesis are different jobs and mixing them made both worse.
A hard call-rate cap (LLM_MAX_CALLS_PER_MIN) over letting the agent run free — an agent with no budget will happily spend real money re-confirming what it already knew.

Rules-based intent extraction on the query (service, timeframe, log level) over sending everything to the model — cheaper, deterministic, and it turns a vague question into a scoped retrieval before any token is spent.
challenges: Repetitive log lines drowned retrieval — a service emitting the same error thousands of times returned thousands of near-identical results and starved the context window. Solved with signature clustering, so a recurring template is one clustered result with counts and a time range instead of thousands of copies.

The original loop carried its control flow in flags spread across a single large function, which made resume logic replay message history and accumulate compatibility hacks. Extracting an explicit state object and declared transitions turned resume into load-state-and-dispatch, and made each phase independently testable.
Embedding cost and latency sat directly on the ingest path — moved behind the background worker with offset tracking, and a Redis cache layer keeps repeated work out of the hot path.

Scoping an investigation that begins with no known time bound — fixed windows either missed the cause or buried it. The progressive expansion ladder made scope something the loop discovers rather than something the user has to guess.
improvements: Distribute ingestion across nodes — the single-machine design is deliberate, but it's also the first thing to hit at real log volume.
Broaden the eval sets beyond the scripted investigation datasets — RAGAS scores are only as honest as the scenarios behind them.
Push cross-encoder reranking across every retrieval path, not just the primary one, so precision doesn't depend on which view the agent queried.

questions: How do you know the retrieval is any good?
Why hybrid search instead of pure vector retrieval?
Why a hand-rolled state machine instead of LangGraph?
Why does it run entirely locally?
How does it decide how far back in time to look?
Why Postgres instead of a dedicated vector database?

projects.title: collapser-grpc
projects.details: An open-source Go sidecar that kills thundering herds. When thousands of callers ask for the same thing at the same moment, exactly one request reaches the backend and everyone else attaches to that result — schema-agnostic, zero-allocation on the hot path, with Prometheus metrics out of the box.
projects.architecture: The proxy sits between clients and a gRPC backend. Each arriving request is keyed by SHA256(method + payload), checked against a 100ms TTL result cache, then against the in-flight map. The first caller for a key becomes the leader and calls the backend on a detached context; every later caller becomes a follower and waits on that same result, which is broadcast to all of them on completion. A passthrough codec forwards raw gRPC frames without ever needing service descriptors, so it works against any protobuf service with zero schema knowledge. One persistent *grpc.ClientConn is held for the life of the process, so every request rides existing HTTP/2 streams instead of paying for a handshake. Streaming RPCs are detected and bypassed, panics are recovered, and shutdown drains in-flight work.
design_decisions: A sidecar rather than a client library — collapsing has to work for every caller in the mesh regardless of language. A Go library only ever helps the Go services.
A passthrough codec over decoding requests — forwarding raw frames means no proto descriptors, no code generation, no redeploy when a schema changes. The proxy is genuinely schema-agnostic.

Detached-context semantics for the leader's backend call — this is the explicit improvement over golang.org/x/sync/singleflight, where the leader cancelling takes down work that other callers are still waiting on. Here the backend call outlives whichever client happened to arrive first.
SHA256 over method + payload as the collapse key — identical requests hash identically without the proxy understanding a single field.
Errors are not cached by default — a transient blip should not be replayed to every caller for a full TTL window. Negative caching exists but is opt-in via COLLAPSER_CACHE_ERRORS.
One persistent ClientConn instead of per-request dialing — HTTP/2 multiplexing does the work, and TCP/TLS handshakes disappear from the hot path.
tradeoffs: Followers inherit the leader's failure — one backend error fails everyone attached. That's the correct read-through semantic, and retrying per-follower would recreate the exact herd the proxy exists to prevent.
A 100ms result TTL trades a small, bounded staleness window for the collapse ratio — long enough to absorb a burst, short enough that nobody is served genuinely old data.
Streaming RPCs are bypassed rather than half-supported — a stream has no single result to fan out, so client-streaming and bidirectional calls are detected and passed straight through.
Everything is configured by environment variable rather than a config file or control plane — a sidecar should be deployable without shipping a second artifact alongside it.
challenges: Client cancellation killing shared work — the naive implementation runs the backend call on the leader's context, so when that client disconnected every follower died with it. Detaching the context fixed it, and it's the core reason this exists rather than a singleflight wrapper.
Server-streaming RPCs are indistinguishable from unary ones without a proto descriptor — a known, documented limitation: server-streaming calls currently return only the first response frame.
TLS to the backend uses the system trust store — custom CA bundles and mutual TLS aren't supported yet, which rules out some zero-trust meshes today.
improvements: Optional proto descriptors so server-streaming RPCs can be detected and passed through correctly, closing the one real correctness gap.
Mutual TLS and custom CA bundle support for backends that don't chain to the system trust store.
Per-method collapse policy — everything is global today, and non-idempotent methods deserve an explicit opt-out rather than relying on the TTL being short.

highlights: Prometheus metrics and structured logging built in
questions: What is request collapsing and when does it help?
How is this different from singleflight?
Why a sidecar instead of a client library?
How does it work without knowing the protobuf schema?

projects.title: Fend
projects.details: A desktop tool for hardening Ubuntu fleets. Security modules are written as Ansible playbooks and pushed to grouped remote hosts over SSH, so an operator can apply a hardening standard across many machines from one GUI — with per-run logging and no agent installed on the targets.
projects.architecture: An Electron application with a React and TypeScript renderer drives Ansible underneath. Hosts are organized into inventory groups so hardening can be applied per environment rather than per machine, and authentication to targets is key-based rather than interactive. Security modules ship as playbooks, custom scripts can be added alongside the built-in set, and every run is logged so an operator can see what was applied where.
design_decisions: Ansible as the execution layer over a custom agent — it is agentless and idempotent, so hardening can be re-applied safely and targets need nothing installed. Re-running a playbook converging to the same state is exactly the property a hardening tool needs.

Playbooks as the unit of a security module — operators can read, audit, and extend a module without touching application code, which matters when the thing being changed is a machine's security posture.
Host grouping over per-machine operation — hardening standards apply to environments, not individual boxes, and grouping is what makes the tool usable beyond a handful of hosts.
A desktop GUI over a web service — the tool holds SSH access to production hosts, so keeping it on the operator's machine avoids standing up a privileged always-on service.
Key-based authentication to clients rather than prompting for credentials on every run.
tradeoffs: Ubuntu-focused rather than distro-agnostic — the playbooks encode Ubuntu-specific package and config paths, which keeps modules concrete at the cost of portability.
A desktop app means no central audit trail across operators — logs live per-run on the machine that ran them.
Coverage is scoped to the implemented modules rather than a full CIS benchmark, so it reduces attack surface without claiming certification against a standard.
challenges: Making remote execution legible in a GUI — an operator needs to know what a hardening run changed on which hosts, which drove per-run logging rather than fire-and-forget execution.
Bridging a desktop UI to an automation tool designed for the terminal, without hiding the playbooks that make the behavior auditable.
improvements: Validate against more Ubuntu versions, and expand the module set for broader security coverage.
Map modules to recognized benchmarks (such as CIS) so a run can be reported against a standard.
Dynamic inventory and in-app script editing, so hosts and modules can change without leaving the tool.

questions: What does system hardening actually do?
Why Ansible instead of a custom agent?
How does it scale past a handful of hosts?

projects.title: Shrinkr
projects.details: A URL shortener with a Cobra command-line client and a Fiber backend. It supports expiring links, secret-code-protected URLs, and browser-based SSO login, with Redis in front of MongoDB so redirects resolve from cache rather than the database.
projects.architecture: A Cobra CLI handles authentication and link management, talking to a Fiber HTTP backend. Redis fronts MongoDB: short codes resolve from cache on the read path, with MongoDB as the source of truth for link records, ownership, expiry, and protection. Login runs through browser-based Google SSO so credentials never pass through the terminal.
design_decisions: Redis in front of MongoDB rather than a single store — redirection is a read-dominated, latency-sensitive path, and it deserves an in-memory lookup while durable link metadata stays in the database.
A CLI as the primary client — shortening a URL is a one-line action, and a terminal client fits the workflow better than a page load for a developer audience.
Browser-based SSO rather than terminal credential entry — the CLI hands off to the browser for Google auth, so passwords never touch the shell or its history.
Expiry and secret-code protection as first-class link properties rather than bolt-ons, so access control is enforced at resolution time.
tradeoffs: Split client and server repositories — clean separation, but it means two deployables and two things to keep in version step.
Cache-fronted reads accept a small consistency window on link updates in exchange for redirect latency.
A CLI-first client narrows the audience to developers; there is no general web UI.
challenges: Keeping authentication usable in a terminal tool without handling passwords directly, which is what pushed login into the browser SSO flow.
Designing the cache and database split so that expiry and protected-link rules are still enforced when a redirect is served from cache rather than the database.
improvements: Analytics per link (hit counts, referrers) — the obvious next feature for a shortener and a natural fit for the existing Redis layer.
Custom aliases and rate limiting on resolution.
Consolidate the CLI and API repositories, and add end-to-end tests across the two.

highlights: Cobra CLI with browser SSO handoff
questions: How does SSO work from a command-line tool?
What would you change if it had to scale?

experience.summary: Co-built an LLM-driven test configuration generator over 150+ versioned specification documents with a FAISS retrieval layer — 50% less manual authoring across 6+ teams. Also rebuilt the logging pipeline on artifact-backed storage (35% lower stale-artifact cost) and pushed first-pass Kubernetes deployment success from 60% to 95%.

Built performance-run reporting utilities that turned raw worker-node utilization metrics into standardized KPI tables, making resource bottlenecks visible. Refactored the test scheduling dashboard's state management — cut UI support tickets 80% for 75+ engineers.

Architected a modular NestJS LMS backend with role-based access control and an async media pipeline (Bull + FFmpeg) transcoding uploads to adaptive-bitrate HLS — upload-to-stream went from 30 minutes to 5. Secured delivery with a Cloudflare Worker CDN proxy authorizing every HLS segment.
